question: Why does A* use a heuristic instead of expanding every node?

storyboard.learning_goal: Understand that A* uses h(n) estimating distance-to-go to order expansion by f=g+h, so it expands far fewer nodes than blind expansion while still finding an optimal path when h is admissible.
storyboard.driving_question: Why does A* use a heuristic instead of expanding every node?
storyboard.learner_start: Knows grid pathfinding has a start, goal, obstacles, and cost-so-far; has seen blind search expand outward but not why guidance preserves optimality.
storyboard.concrete_example: 7x7 grid trackable case: start bottom-left, goal top-right, vertical wall with one gap; compare expanding outward everywhere vs guided toward goal.
storyboard.representation: Worked execution with aligned comparison on one persistent grid. It fits because the learning difficulty is how ordering changes work: the same map and wall let the viewer attribute fewer expansions to the added heuristic. Capability gap: renderer limited to circle/box/text/arrow/line/path/svg, so cells are boxes, costs are text, frontier is boxes/circles, heuristic is color shade + numbers, no rich terrain or 3D.
assumptions: Grid moves cost 1 per step (4-connected); diagonal not allowed
Heuristic shown is Manhattan distance, admissible for this map

visual_design.why: Blind vs guided expansion on identical map exposes what differs (expansion order/count) and what stays same (map, start, goal, optimal path through gap).
visual_design.misreading: Darker shading or fewer boxes could be read as walls removed or as straight-line movement ignoring cost and wall.
visual_design.safeguard: Keep context wall visible in all beats; label shade legend as estimate not blocked; show path must go around wall through gap, with g counting steps taken.
encodings: box fill = state: light = unvisited, saturated = expanded part, outline = frontier
color shade of probability_dist = heuristic value: lighter near result, darker far
text number = g, h, f for frontier nodes
line/path sampled_output = final path through gap

beats.question: What happens if we expand every node equally?
beats.insight: Blind expansion spreads in all directions, including away from the goal, so work grows with area not direction.
beats.before: Grid context with input_token start bottom-left, result goal top-right, wall with gap in middle; no expansion yet.
beats.change: Wave of part boxes expands outward ring by ring from input_token in all four directions, wrapping around both sides of wall.
beats.after: Large block of expanded part boxes covers much of grid left and below wall, even directions that move away from result.
beats.reasoning: Seeing the same map fill uniformly shows cost of no guidance: effort is spent proving bad directions are bad.
beats.camera: Static wide on full grid to show symmetric spread and wasted area away from goal.
beats.narration: If we have no guess about direction, we must try everywhere equally. Watch how much of the map we fill, even behind the start.
beats.interaction: Ask learner to predict how many squares will be filled before reaching goal.
beats.visual_test: Viewer can point to expanded squares behind start and say they were explored despite leading away from goal.

beats.question: What extra guess does the heuristic add?
beats.insight: Heuristic estimates remaining distance, forming a slope that points toward the goal before we walk it.
beats.before: Same grid with prior expansion faded but wall, start and goal retained.
beats.change: Overlay probability_dist: text Manhattan numbers and light-to-dark shading on each cell, lowest near result, highest far from it, wall cells excluded.
beats.after: Viewer sees a gradient field centered on result, independent of path taken so far.
beats.reasoning: Re-encoding same cells by estimated remainder makes direction visible as shade/number, separate from cost already paid.
beats.camera: Hold grid, focus on numbers and shade gradient near goal vs far corner.
beats.narration: Now add a cheap guess: Manhattan steps left if there were no wall. Lighter means looks closer to the goal. This is not the true cost, just an estimate.
beats.interaction: Ask learner to read two cells: which looks closer by shade and number.
beats.visual_test: Viewer can identify which of two unvisited cells is estimated closer by shade/number without search.

beats.question: How does A* use that guess to skip work?
beats.insight: Ordering by f = g + h expands promising low-total cells first, so search stretches toward the goal and leaves far sides unexpanded.
beats.before: Grid with shade field and start/goal/wall; frontier reset to start.
beats.change: Animate part expansion in f-order: circles/arrows pick lowest f cells first, forming narrow corridor toward gap and to goal; side branches stay light/unexpanded; sampled_output path appears through gap.
beats.after: Narrow expanded corridor vs beat 1 full block side-by-side impression on same map, with final path using gap; counts show e.g. many vs few expansions.
beats.reasoning: Preserving map while changing only expansion order lets viewer attribute fewer expansions to f-ordering, not to changed map.
beats.camera: Static comparison: keep full grid, zoom slightly to corridor and unexpanded region to contrast.
beats.narration: A* still tracks steps taken, g, but adds the guess, h. It always tries the smallest total, f. So it leans toward the goal and skips squares whose total already looks worse.
beats.interaction: Have learner predict next pick between two frontier cells with different g+h.
beats.visual_test: Viewer can explain why a cell toward goal was picked before a closer-to-start cell by comparing f numbers.

beats.question: Why is skipping safe instead of just going straight?
beats.insight: Cells with high f cannot beat the best known total if h never overestimates, so leaving them unexpanded preserves optimality while saving work.
beats.before: Focused corridor and final sampled_output path retained with f values visible.
beats.change: Highlight unexpanded far-side part cells with high f lines showing f >= found path cost; show greedy straight arrow blocked by wall to contrast.
beats.after: Viewer sees skipped region labeled too-expensive-to-be-better, and straight-line move failing at wall, justifying guidance + wall awareness.
beats.reasoning: Enacting the consequence - blocked straight line and too-high f - shows heuristic guides but does not hallucinate through walls; g corrects it.
beats.camera: Focus on skipped region and wall gap, then on final path cost readout.
beats.narration: We cannot just walk straight; the wall blocks us and true cost matters. Because our guess never overestimates, any skipped square with a larger guess-total cannot give a shorter path than the one we found.
beats.interaction: Ask what would happen if h overestimated: show one inflated number would risk skipping the true gap.
beats.visual_test: Viewer can state rule: skip only because f is already worse, and overestimate would break safety.

beats.cameraIntent: Static wide on full grid to show symmetric spread away from goal
Hold grid, focus on shade gradient and numbers near goal vs far corner
Keep full grid, zoom slightly to corridor and unexpanded region to contrast
Focus on skipped region and wall gap, then on final path cost readout

answer: A* uses a heuristic estimate of distance-to-go to order expansions by f=g+h, heading first to nodes most likely on a cheap complete path. This avoids expanding every node equally in all directions. If h never overestimates, any unexpanded node with higher f cannot beat the found path, so A* saves work while staying optimal.
